overview: Here Arran means a medieval Caucasian region between the Kura and Aras rivers, not the Scottish island. The map covers 1000 to 1200, across changing rulers. Its simplified outline includes Barda and Baylaqan but cuts off the Ganja urban area discussed here. This is neither a complete map of ancient Caucasian Albania nor an uninterrupted kingdom; Armenia, Artsakh and later regional identities remain distinct.

periods.title: Shaddadid power in Arran
periods.summary: The Ganja branch governed important regional towns.

periods.title: Seljuq and atabeg authority
periods.summary: Political control changed while cities and literary life continued.

items.text: The Shaddadids established themselves at Ganja in 969 or 970 with local support. Fadl I expanded their territory and took Barda and Baylaqan in 993, shortly before this map begins. Their dynasty probably had Kurdish origins, but its subjects belonged to a much more varied regional population.

In 1075 the Seljuq commander Sav Tegin took the Ganja branch’s territories. Peacock favors the account connecting this transfer to Sultan Malik Shah, rather than the already deceased Alp Arslan. The Shaddadids of Ani followed a separate political history; their survival does not mean their old Arran government survived unchanged.

An earthquake devastated Ganja in 1139, and a Georgian army raided the damaged city. The governor Qara Sonqor rebuilt it, and Ganja again flourished under later rulers, including the Ildegizid atabegs. Rebuilding a city meant restoring a place where people worked and lived, as well as a seat of power.

One iron gate preserves a craftsman’s name. Its Arabic inscription dates its manufacture to AH 455, about 1063, and names the blacksmith Ibrahim son of Uthman. Georgian forces carried the gate away in 1139; a surviving leaf is now at Gelati. A city entrance became a war trophy, but the maker’s credit survived the journey.

sections.title: Ovens, workshops and the archaeology of ordinary life

items.text: Excavations at Barda in 2015 uncovered settlement from the eleventh through fourteenth centuries. This challenged the idea that everyone had abandoned the city for nearby Ganja. Pottery and building remains can correct a story of urban decline: losing political importance is not the same as losing every household.

Barda’s earliest medieval layers in the 2016 report were dated by pottery to the eleventh through early thirteenth centuries. One hearth reused large fired bricks or floor tiles and retained ash from its last use. A useful old building material could begin another career beside somebody’s fire.

Nearby, archaeologists found a clay-lined tandir oven on a brick foundation and a pot buried in the ground, probably for cooking or storage. They tentatively interpreted the setting as an outdoor domestic area. These are practical traces of preparing and keeping food; the remains do not identify a particular family or recipe.

The 2017 Barda report records iron blades and tools, reworked glazed pottery, faience beads, cowrie shells and a worked bone handle. These finds come from a range of medieval contexts, some beyond this map’s endpoint. They reveal skilled hands cutting, shaping and reusing small objects as well as building monuments.

Small scale pans and coins from the same excavation suggest trading activity. The report cannot turn them into a named shop with a price list, but weighing equipment makes the business of exchange tangible. A tiny balance could matter as much to a transaction as a large city gate.

Tenth-century geographers, describing Baylaqan just before this map’s window, praised a flourishing town on the route between Ardabil and Barda. It produced textiles and a confection called natef. The report preserves a tempting trace of regional food, although it does not supply a recipe or tell us how often children ate it.

Letters and documents associated with the official Masud ibn Namdar in 1111 and 1112 illuminate Baylaqan’s ethnically and religiously mixed society. Such paperwork offers a view of people living under government, alongside the chronicles that mostly follow rulers and campaigns. Arran was not a place where everyone shared one language or faith.

David of Gandzak, writing around the early twelfth century, criticized Christian women at Ganja who married Kurdish men. Yet his account also describes priests baptizing their children and continuing religious care. Read critically, his disapproval reveals actual mixed families and mothers passing on traditions across boundaries that religious authorities wanted to maintain.

sections.title: Stories and a real line of Persian

items.text: Nizami of Ganja became famous for five long narrative poems, later collected as the Khamsa, or quintet. He drew on earlier Persian writing, oral traditions and Arabic stories while reshaping them into new works. Later poets imitated both individual poems and the five-part collection, carrying Ganja’s literary influence far beyond Arran.

A modern scholarly printing of Nizami’s Layli and Majnun, completed in 1188, gives this Persian opening: “ای نام تو بهترین سرآغاز” (ey nām-e to behtarīn sarāghāz). Zahra Taheri translates it “O your name the most rightful beginning.” This is a devotional address. The sample is Persian literary writing from a named poet, not a claim that all Arran’s inhabitants spoke Persian or could read it.

The five poems were gathered into manuscripts after Nizami’s death. The oldest dated surviving copy of the whole collection is from 1362, although earlier incomplete copies survive. This later manuscript history matters: the writing sample above is transmitted literature, not a photograph of a page in the poet’s own handwriting.

ending.text: The atlas stops in 1200, before further political upheaval. Mongol forces devastated Baylaqan in the early 1220s, but survivors returned and rebuilt; later attempts to revive the town also followed. Arran’s cities and regional names changed over time. Neither the map endpoint nor the destruction of a town marks the disappearance of all its inhabitants.
